clue.text: Fewer than 1,000 instruments will enthral Mozart?

definitions.note: an example of the answer, flagged by the question mark

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece holds the other inside it

blocks.note: wind instruments, the woodwind and brass of an orchestra
fewer than a number is under it
K is the abbreviation for a thousand

explanation.surface: A musical query: the orchestra's instruments will captivate Mozart, but there are fewer than a thousand of them.
explanation.walkthrough: K is the standard abbreviation for a thousand; the definition is a famous example, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Mozart composed and performed brilliantly as a small child, the classic example of a prodigy who achieves greatness very young.

clue.text: Buzz is started by internet game inventor

blocks.note: the web is the internet
to give someone a buzz or a bell is to phone them
taken as written

explanation.surface: Online excitement surrounds the person who invented a game.
explanation.walkthrough: Buzz is started by internet: WEB comes first, then BELL IS. William WEBB ELLIS is credited with picking up the ball in a football match at Rugby School, inventing rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend credits this Rugby School pupil with creating rugby football in 1823, when he ran carrying the ball.

clue.text: Book inspired by recent sci-fi work? You can bet on it

indicators.note: to be inspired is to be breathed into, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: recent means new
Mark is a book of the New Testament
E.T. is Spielberg's science-fiction film

explanation.surface: A novel drawing its ideas from a new science-fiction work turns out to be a safe wager.
explanation.walkthrough: NEWMARKET is the Suffolk town that is the home of British horse racing, and also a card game played for stakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Horses race at this famous English racecourse, where punters place wagers, and the card game of the same name is played for money.

clue.text: Crew on a certain film that involves skirted, cavorting men

definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for a dance

blocks.note: a rowing eight is a crew
some, as in 'some person', means a certain one
a reel of film

explanation.surface: A film crew shooting a movie about men in skirts prancing about.
explanation.walkthrough: The skirts are kilts: an EIGHTSOME REEL is a Scottish country dance for eight people, often danced by kilted men.
explanation.definitionFit: This lively Scottish dance for eight dancers is typically performed at ceilidhs by participants wearing kilts, the skirted men.

clue.text: Renounce evil – it’s what financial contributor does

blocks.note: to kick a habit is to give it up
sin is evil

explanation.surface: A moral exhortation to give up wickedness, oddly linked to someone making a donation.
explanation.walkthrough: KICK SIN, read with the space moved, is KICKS IN.
explanation.definitionFit: To kick in is an informal phrasal verb for contributing money towards a shared cost or fund.

clue.text: What topless person has without hesitation? It’s a walk in the park

indicators.note: without means lacking, so something is taken away

blocks.note: someone bare above the waist has no top on, so no jumper
er is the sound of hesitating

explanation.surface: A riddle about a half-naked person, followed by the reassurance that something is easy.
explanation.walkthrough: A topless person has NO SWEATER; take away ER and NO SWEAT remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal idioms describing a task that is very easy and causes no difficulty or effort.

clue.text: Thomas Becket’s opening part of crypt

indicators.note: an opening is the start of something, so only its first letter is kept

blocks.note: Tom is short for Thomas
the initial of the surname

explanation.surface: The archbishop Thomas Becket begins a section of a church's underground vault.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads naturally as Becket's tomb in Canterbury, which is very apt: he was murdered in the cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: A crypt beneath a church holds burial places, so a grave chamber is one part of it.

clue.text: Like an egg adult removed from two different ducks

indicators.note: something removed from a word is taken out of it

blocks.note: the first sense of ducks: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, O
the second sense of ducks: dodges
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: An egg-shaped description, then a grown bird taken from two kinds of duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ducks' is used twice over: O (a zero score in cricket) and AVOID (dodges); remove A from AVOID and put it after O.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovoid is an adjective from Latin ovum, meaning shaped roughly oval, with the form of a hen's egg.

clue.text: Republican outrage led by president who’s a criminal?

blocks.note: either President Bush
R abbreviates Republican
outrage is anger

explanation.surface: Republican fury fronted by a president who may be a crook, a political swipe.
explanation.walkthrough: Bush was himself a Republican president, which makes the surface hang together neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: A bushranger was an outlaw in colonial Australia who lived in the bush and robbed travellers.

clue.text: Great houses retired cruciverbalists equip with a rug

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the letters run backwards
a house holds things, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: great means big
crossword setters refer to themselves as we

explanation.surface: Stately homes where elderly crossword fans fit out a room with a carpet.
explanation.walkthrough: Rug is slang for a hairpiece, so to bewig someone is to put a wig on them.
explanation.definitionFit: Rug is informal slang for a toupee or wig, and to bewig means to provide someone with one.

clue.text: Leading figure in country cuts agricultural output

blocks.note: Johnny Cash, a leading country music singer
to crop is to cut short

explanation.surface: A national leader reduces farm production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' suggests a nation, but it is country music, and its leading figure is Johnny Cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Cash crops are those grown for sale rather than for the farmer's own use, a kind of farm produce.

clue.text: Evil-doers receiving a lesson if reforming … in these?

definitions.text: Evil-doers receiving a lesson if reforming … in these?

indicators.note: reforming means re-shaping, so the letters take a new form
to receive is to take in, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: cons are convicts, criminals
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Wrongdoers may be taught a lesson when they reform, perhaps in these places.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole the clue describes the answer: sinners in a confessional receive absolution and counsel as they reform.
explanation.definitionFit: Confessionals are the booths in a church where penitent sinners confess to a priest seeking forgiveness.

clue.text: Amazing star, i.e. captivating West End in theatre

definitions.text: Amazing star, i.e. captivating West End in theatre

indicators.note: something amazing is bewildering, so the letters are thrown into confusion
to captivate is to hold captive, so one piece is held inside
the end of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A stunning performer enthralling audiences in London's theatreland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' looks like London's theatre district but gives just the last letter of 'West'; the whole clue then describes a theatre performer.
explanation.definitionFit: An artiste is a professional entertainer such as a singer or dancer, and a star of the stage is one.

clue.text: Dare maybe to back firm exposed in worst moment

indicators.note: to go back is to run in the opposite direction
exposed means stripped of its covering, so the outer letters go

blocks.note: Dan Dare, the space hero of the Eagle comic
the inside of the word

explanation.surface: Daring, perhaps, to support a company caught out at its lowest point.
explanation.walkthrough: Dan Dare was a famous British comic-strip space pilot; 'maybe' signals that Dare is an example of a DAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is literally the lowest point beneath an observer, and figuratively the lowest point of fortune.

clue.text: Little boxer who fails to box sulks? Punch may be seen here

indicators.note: a fighter failing in the ring is knocked all over the place, so the letters end up jumbled

blocks.note: a young boxer dog is a pup
pets are fits of sulking
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A young boxer who will not fight sulks; a punch might be seen here.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch is not a blow but Mr Punch of Punch and Judy, the traditional seaside puppet show; 'boxer' is a breed of dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Punch is the glove-puppet star of Punch and Judy, so he appears in this kind of entertainment.

clue.text: Elon ultimately bores country with present name X?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept
to bore is to drill into, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: the final letter of the name
the United Kingdom
the present moment is now
N abbreviates name

explanation.surface: A jibe at Elon Musk boring a country with Twitter's new name, X.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thoughts of Musk's rebranded platform, but X is the algebraic symbol for an unknown quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: In algebra the letter X conventionally stands for a quantity whose value is not yet found.

clue.text: US capital payment banked in great quantity

indicators.note: money banked is deposited inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: tons of something is a lot
rent is a regular payment

explanation.surface: American money: a payment deposited in a large sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' tempts a financial reading, but it is a state capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Trenton is the state capital city of New Jersey, so it is a capital in the United States.

clue.text: Fancy attire? Son dresses down

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are decked out in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fancy dress? The boy chooses to wear something casual instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dresses down' looks like more clothing talk, but here it means scolds.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress someone down is to rebuke them severely, and tearing into someone is an equivalent idiom for harsh criticism.

clue.text: What aimless person does for Harry, Graham and Dennis?

blocks.note: first meaning: idles about doing nothing much
second meaning: people sharing one surname

explanation.walkthrough: Harry Potter the boy wizard, Graham Potter the football manager and Dennis Potter the TV playwright share the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: To potter is to occupy oneself in a desultory way, and the three famous people all bear that family name.

clue.text: One that’s fired, shockingly, conned figure in Paris

blocks.note: to be stung is to be swindled
un is French for one

explanation.surface: Someone shockingly sacked, swindled by a character in the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' and 'shockingly' suggest a scandalous dismissal, but they describe a weapon that delivers an electric shock.
explanation.definitionFit: A stun gun is discharged at a target and immobilises it with an electric shock, hence fired shockingly.

clue.text: Label in old garment one’s grabbed to make money

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: hose are old-fashioned stockings or breeches
a tag is a label

explanation.surface: A label inside a vintage piece of clothing, snatched to be sold for profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grabbed to make money' suggests theft for resale; it is kidnapping for ransom.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostage is a person seized and held so that a ransom can be demanded for their release.

clue.text: Play courtier in half hour before five to ten, say

blocks.note: the first half of the word
five to ten, 5:10, is an example of a ratio

explanation.surface: A theatre fan plays at court in a half-hour slot just before ten to ten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Five to ten' looks like a clock time but is a ratio; 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio is Hamlet's loyal friend, a courtier at Elsinore in Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: Say where to find Kingdom of Jordan’s subject

blocks.note: the answer to 'where?' begins 'the ...', naming the place
Jordan lies in the Middle East, abbreviated ME

explanation.surface: A question about where a Jordanian citizen can be found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject' looks like a citizen of the kingdom, but it is the topic; THE ME stands for the Middle East.
explanation.definitionFit: The theme of a talk or essay is its central topic, which is its subject.

clue.text: See 1
Group providing deliveries entertaining cricketer pulls out of the ground

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: UPS, United Parcel Service, is a delivery company
Joe Root, the England batsman

explanation.surface: A delivery firm hosting a cricketer who leaves the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' and 'cricketer' suggest bowling, but UPS is the parcel firm; 'the ground' is soil, not a cricket ground.
explanation.definitionFit: To uproot a plant is to drag it from the soil, roots and all.

clue.text: Renaissance writer‘s repeated adverbial addition

indicators.note: something repeated is given a second time, so the same piece appears twice in a row

blocks.note: -ly is the suffix added to make an adverb
the same suffix again

explanation.surface: A literary note that an Elizabethan author is just an adverb ending said twice.
explanation.walkthrough: John Lyly was an Elizabethan writer, best known for Euphues.
explanation.definitionFit: John Lyly was an English author of prose romances and court plays in the sixteenth century.

clue.text: Dawn running behind Henry

indicators.note: behind means coming after, so the first-named piece is sent to the back

blocks.note: Hal is a pet form of Henry, as with Prince Hal
running away is flight

explanation.surface: A woman called Dawn jogging along after a man named Henry.
explanation.walkthrough: Dawn looks like a name, but it is daybreak.
explanation.definitionFit: At dawn there is only dim, partial illumination before full daylight, which is half-light.

clue.text: Some plates I won’t put out

indicators.note: to plate is to coat with metal, so one piece is covered by another

blocks.note: any means some
a refusal is no

explanation.surface: A refusal to clear away some of the dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plates' looks like crockery but is a verb meaning coats; 'put out' looks like setting the table but means irritate.
explanation.definitionFit: To be put out is to be irritated or upset, so putting someone out means to irritate them.

clue.text: Perhaps bath is no longer hot

blocks.note: what no longer is, was
H is the tap abbreviation for hot

explanation.surface: A complaint that the bathwater has gone cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a grumble about bathwater; 'perhaps' marks a bath as one example of a wash.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a bath is one way of cleaning oneself, an example of having a wash.

clue.text: Politician’s demise over singular remark drawing a conclusion

indicators.note: over means covering, so one piece is placed around another

blocks.note: a politician's demise is the end of a Conservative, a Tory
S abbreviates singular

explanation.surface: A politician's downfall over one peculiar comment that wraps things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' looks like 'strange' but is the grammar abbreviation S.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said to close a discussion firmly, signalling there is nothing more to be said.
